judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Short alarm barks with a native slip ('look out' for lookout) and the plain 'curse of the necromancer come to haunt Nox again'; reads like a siege-chapter guard.

items.label: B
items.critique: The over-courteous welcome with 'fairest of all villages in the land of Nox' and 'open warm arms of aid' is the campaign's earnest, slightly stilted gate speech; the flat closing line fits.

items.label: C
items.critique: Clipped 'Sorry.' then a reason, a curt 'Move on!' and a one-line release; plain and functional in the Nox way.

items.label: D
items.critique: Faction-hostile checkpoint with an unpunctuated vocative ('Be gone [Group], before I blast you') and a terse closing; native roughness.

items.label: E
items.critique: Stacks three exclamations and reuses another guard's direction line word for word; the 'boy' farewell with a bandit warning feels assembled from parts rather than spoken.

items.label: F
items.critique: Two lines that say the same thing (foreman waits at the mines) and a grand 'Your valor knows no peer' thanks; more a quest-briefing relay than a guard's bark.

items.label: G
items.critique: Plausible jailer barks with an escalation gag, but the page break after a four-word welcome and the neat three-step build feel designed.

items.label: H
items.critique: Functional directions, but the 'spoken to again' and 'later' lines are near-duplicates with added routing detail, which reads like a writer filling slots.

items.label: I
items.critique: The rule-list joke and the 'Oh, I forgot to mention' afterthought are a little too polished as comedy; Nox's guard humour is usually blunter.

items.label: J
items.critique: Lore-proud civic lines with a dropped article ('can be dangerous place') typical of the shipped text; no attempt at a joke.

tells: Westwood's guards carry small native slips (missing commas before a vocative, a dropped article, 'look out' split) and rarely restate the same information twice; the new texts are clean and tend to repeat a direction across the 'again' and 'later' slots.
New texts cluster several exclamations and a quest-giver's urgency into a guard ('Lives are at stake!', 'Your valor knows no peer'), where Westwood's guards stay in a narrow gatekeeper role.
Comedy in the new texts is built as a setup and a tidy afterthought; Westwood's humour is flatter and incidental.
Lines lifted verbatim from one text into another (same sentence frame for directions) suggest imitation of exemplars.
